title: The Cars That Did Not Stop
text:
In 2012 Paul Piff and his colleagues at Berkeley published seven studies on social class and ethics. The best known took place at street crossings in the San Francisco Bay Area. Observers stood at a busy four-way intersection and at a pedestrian crosswalk, coding the make, age and look of each car, and noting whether its driver cut in front of other cars or failed to yield to a pedestrian, as California law requires.

Drivers of the most expensive, high-status cars were more likely to cut off other drivers and to drive through the crosswalk while a person, actually a member of the research team, was waiting to cross. Drivers of the cheapest cars almost always stopped.

In laboratory studies, the team found that people who saw themselves as higher in class were more willing to lie in a negotiation, cheat in a game to win a prize, and even take candy meant for children. They also held more favorable attitudes toward greed. When lower-class participants were led to think about the benefits of greed, they too behaved less ethically. The authors argued that privilege and independence from others can weaken attention to the rules that protect them.
lesson: Status and resources can quietly convince people that the rules are for others. Those who rise should guard their own behavior most carefully.
location: San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA
source: Piff, P. K., Stancato, D. M., Cote, S., Mendoza-Denton, R., and Keltner, D. (2012). Higher social class predicts increased unethical behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(11), 4086-4091.
caveat: Later replications, including a large Dutch survey study, found weak or opposite links between class and unethical behavior, so the result is not settled.
